report:
Conclusion: **qualified yes**—olive leaf extract (OLE), especially oleuropein/phenolic-rich products, appears capable of **modestly lowering blood pressure** in some adults with pre- or stage-1 hypertension, but the evidence base is small and not strong enough to replace prescribed treatment.

Human trials are suggestive: a randomized double-blind crossover trial of phenolic-rich OLE reported BP improvements in at-risk adults (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486627/), and an Indonesian trial found OLE 500 mg twice daily lowered systolic/diastolic BP comparably to captopril in stage-1 hypertension (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/). A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs supports cardiovascular-risk effects including BP, while still reflecting limited, heterogeneous trials (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y). By contrast, EFSA’s 2011 opinion did **not** substantiate an olive-polyphenol claim for maintaining normal blood pressure, underscoring regulatory caution (https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.2903/j.efsa.2011.2033).

Practical takeaway: OLE may be a reasonable adjunct for mildly elevated BP, but effects are likely modest, product standardization varies, and it can add to antihypertensive effects. Do not stop medication; monitor BP and discuss with a clinician, especially if pregnant, on BP/diabetes drugs, or with kidney disease.
